alt_method_summary: Bhagavad Gītā 9.27–28 (with 8.7): whatever one does, eats, offers in the fire, gives or performs as austerity is to be done as an offering to the Lord; thus one is released from the bonds of action with their good and bad fruits and, yoked in oneself by the yoga of renunciation (saṃnyāsa-yoga-yuktātmā), freed, comes to him; mind and intellect offered to him.

Whatever one does, eats, offers, gives or practises as austerity, do it as an offering to the Lord, mentally renouncing all actions in him; one is thereby freed from the bonds of action with good and evil fruits.

Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Those who resign all actions to the Lord (mayi saṃnyasya), holding him supreme, and worship him meditating with undivided yoga (12.6) — for them, whose awareness (cetas) is set on him, he becomes before long the deliverer from the ocean of death and saṃsāra (12.7).

name: Performing dharma as an offering to the Lord (īśvarārpaṇa)
method_summary: Doing the enjoined acts with the thought of offering them to Śrī Govinda (Āpadeva) or Īśvara (Laugākṣi Bhāskara), which makes dharma a cause of the highest good; the Gītā's 'whatever you do, do it as an offering to me' is cited as authority.

name: Devotion to wakefulness
method_summary: Purifying the mind by walking and sitting through the day and the first and last watches of the night, lying down mindfully in the middle watch in the lion's posture (MN 39; MN 107).

name: Initiation into mendicancy (dīkṣā)
method_summary: The candidate, with family consent, renounces possessions in a public ceremony, receives the mendicant's equipment (whisk, bowls or water-pot) and a new name, takes the vow of equanimity for life, and has the hair plucked; Śvetāmbaras later confer the 'great initiation' (chedopasthāpanā) with the five vows; Digambara men become naked monks after the stages of kṣullaka and ailaka.

name: Friendliness, delight, compassion and equanimity (Tattvārtha 7.11)
method_summary: Friendliness towards all living beings, delight in those superior in virtue, compassion for the afflicted and equanimity towards the undisciplined.

name: Pilgrimage to the tīrthas
method_summary: Pilgrimage on foot to the places of the kalyāṇakas and nirvāṇas and to great temple-hills — Sammeda Śikhara (Pārasnāth), Śatruñjaya (Pālitāṇā), Girnār, Pāvāpurī, Aṣṭāpada (in memory), Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa, Ābu, Rāṇakpur — often with vows and fasting; the 'six-rule' (cha'rī pālit) sangha pilgrimage imitates mendicant discipline.

equivalents.note: pilgrimage to sacred places in the Vedic traditions

name: Jālandharabandha (the throat lock)
method_summary: Contracting the throat and setting the chin firmly on the chest (HYP 3.70; GS 3.12; ŚS 4.38; DYŚ 126; GŚ 36). It binds the network of channels and the 'water of the sky', so that the nectar falling from the moon (or the thousand-petalled lotus) is not consumed by the fire at the navel; it stops the two side channels and binds the sixteen supports (HYP 3.71-73; GS 3.12; DYŚ 127-128). In breath-control it is applied at the end of inhalation (HYP 2.45).
signs_of_progress: destroys old age and death and the host of throat ailments (HYP 3.70-71)
the nectar is not burnt by the fire and the breath is not disturbed (HYP 3.72; GŚ 36)
practised six months one becomes an adept (GS 3.13)

name: Wrangling and cavilling to protect truth
method_summary: Using contentious debate — including quibbles and futile rejoinders, or pure refutation without a counter-thesis — only to protect an ascertained truth from opponents, as a fence of thorny branches protects seedlings.

warnings.text: Quibbles, futile rejoinders and points of defeat are defined so that they can be avoided in one's own speech and exposed in the opponent's (NBh 1.1.1); vitaṇḍā without any purpose collapses into prattle.

name: Service and worship of the jaṅgama
method_summary: Honouring, feeding and serving the wandering Śivayogins (jaṅgamas), whose sight, touch and worship sanctify, and giving them the fruits of one's work.

name: Purification rite for the dead (byang chog)
method_summary: A rite with the peaceful and wrathful deities using the deceased's name card, to purify obscurations, guide the consciousness and burn the card as a sign of release.

name: Pacification for an inauspicious birth
method_summary: When a child is born at an eclipse, at the new moon, at a solar ingress, in Mūla or at a junction (gaṇḍānta) of asterisms, under Viṣṭi, or with other ominous features, a pacification is performed: images of the ruling deities in gold, silver or lead are installed on a vessel, worshipped with the mantras of one's own domestic ritual, bathed over the family and honoured with oblations, followed by feeding brahmins.

name: Mantra repetition (japa)
method_summary: The repetition of a mantra received from a teacher — a seed syllable, the praṇava, a divine name, a Vedic verse or a longer formula — with attention to its sound and meaning. Before repetition the practitioner states the mantra's seer, metre and deity (viniyoga) and places its parts on the body (nyāsa); the count is kept on a rosary (akṣamālā) or the finger-joints. It is done aloud (vācika), whispered (upāṃśu) or mentally (mānasa), each far superior to the previous; Patañjali joins repetition to contemplation of its meaning (YS 1.28). A course of fixed counts with supplementary rites (puraścaraṇa) 'masters' a mantra for use.
prerequisites: a mantra received from a qualified guru (for Āgamic mantras)
purity, a fixed seat and time
signs_of_progress: the mantra 'awakens' and gives fruit (ŚT 2.60–63)
the inward consciousness is realized and obstacles vanish (YS 1.29)
the deity, praised by japa, is pleased and gives enjoyment and liberation (Padmanābhīya quoted in the Padārthādarśa)

warnings.text: A mantra wrong in tone or letter does not convey the meaning intended; as a verbal thunderbolt it harms the sacrificer.
Mantras with defects such as being 'cut' do not protect the practitioner; they must first be purified.
The mantra being repeated is to be kept secret (gopana).
In mental japa one should not move head, neck, tongue or lips.
Recitation done with desire, pride or wrongly leads to lesser worlds, not to Brahman (as taught in the Jāpaka story).

name: Kṛṣṇa-Jayantī fast

name: The five masteries of jhāna (vasī)
method_summary: Practising adverting to, attaining, resolving the duration of, emerging from and reviewing a jhāna wherever, whenever and for as long as one wishes, before going on to the next.

name: Jihvā-śodhana (cleansing — and lengthening — the tongue)
method_summary: The root of the tongue is cleaned with three fingers inserted into the throat to remove phlegm (GS 1.30). RESTRICTED in part: the text goes on to describe rubbing the tongue with butter, 'milking' it and drawing it out with an iron instrument daily at sunrise so that it lengthens (GS 1.31-32) — a preparation for khecarī; that procedure is not reproduced.

name: Worship of the Jina image (jina-pūjā)
method_summary: The householder bathes the consecrated image and offers eight substances — water, sandalwood paste, flowers, incense, lamp, unbroken rice, sweets and fruit (the aṣṭaprakārī pūjā) — with verses recalling the Jina's qualities, followed by inner worship (caityavandana, praise, meditation). The Digambara Terāpantha offers only non-living, dry substances; mendicants perform only inner worship. The Jina, being liberated, does not respond; the worshipper is purified by recalling his qualities.

warnings.text: Sthānakavāsīs and Terāpanthīs reject material worship because it harms one-sensed beings (water, flowers, fire); Mūrtipūjaka teachers restrict material worship to householders.

equivalents.note: outwardly similar image worship, but the Jina is not a grace-giving deity and receives nothing

alt_method_summary: Bathing the image and offering the eight substances — water, sandal paste, flowers (Digambara: yellow rice), incense, lamp, unbroken rice, sweets and fruit — with hymns; 'material worship' (dravya-pūjā) is a support for 'inner worship' (bhāva-pūjā), the contemplation of the Jina's qualities; the Jina does not respond, the worshipper is purified.
notes: The Sthānakavāsī and Śvetāmbara Terāpanthī traditions reject image worship; the Digambara Terāpantha rejects offerings of flowers and fresh produce and the bhaṭṭārakas' ritual authority (recalled).

name: Renovation and re-consecration (jīrṇoddhāra)
method_summary: Rites for repairing a temple or replacing a damaged image, moving the deity's presence temporarily into a pot or substitute (bālālaya) and re-installing it.

name: Entering living samādhi (cīva camāti)
method_summary: Summary only: the tradition's account that a Siddhar, at the end, enters samādhi and is enclosed alive in a shrine, remaining present there. Recorded as the tradition's account; no instructions.
notes: Restricted (ends in death); belief recorded, no procedure.

name: Śrāddha for oneself while living
method_summary: A śrāddha performed for oneself during life (by those without heirs or seeking release), taught in LiP 2.45 and the Pretakalpa (ch. 8, 'self-śrāddha').
notes: Chapter titles checked (LiP 2.45 'jīvacchrāddhavidhi'; GP 2.8 'śrāddhakartr-ātmaśrāddha'); contents not read; no teaching extracted yet.

name: Combining knowledge with works
method_summary: Continuing the Vedic and social duties of one's station throughout life together with meditation on Brahman, rather than renouncing works after knowledge.

name: Jñāna mudrā / cin-mudrā (the gesture of knowledge)
method_summary: The tips of thumb and index finger joined and the other fingers extended, turned to the side — the gesture of knowledge held by teaching deities such as Sarasvatī and Dakṣiṇāmūrti; the commentary distinguishes a related 'exposition gesture' (vyākhyāna-mudrā) (Śāradātilaka, commentary on ch. 6 and ch. 7).

name: Veneration of scripture (Jñāna Pañcamī / Śruta Pañcamī)
method_summary: Once a year manuscripts and books are cleaned, displayed and worshipped: Śvetāmbaras on the fifth of bright Kārttika (Jñāna Pañcamī), Digambaras on the fifth of bright Jyeṣṭha (Śruta Pañcamī), the day the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama was completed and worshipped.

name: Breath-control as knowledge
method_summary: Exhalation as negating the world or renouncing objects, inhalation as 'I am Brahman' or scriptural knowledge, retention as steadiness in realization (Tejobindu 1.31–33; Varāha 5.58).

queries: e-text refs of prc:jnana-pranayama
checks.note: The inline refs and paraphrased content were checked against the e-text passages read for the teachings. All 2 teachings it rests on exist and were located in the e-text.

name: The sacrifice of knowledge (jñāna-yajña)
method_summary: Bhagavad Gītā 4.28, 4.33–34: offering knowledge as sacrifice; better than material sacrifice, since all action culminates in knowledge; the knowledge is learned from knowers who have seen the truth, approached with prostration, questioning and service.
prerequisites: faith, intentness and restraint of the senses (4.39)
signs_of_progress: freedom from delusion; seeing all beings in the self and in the Lord (4.35)
supreme peace (4.39)

Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch07-09): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

alt_method_summary: Bhagavad Gītā 7–9: Some worship the Lord by sacrificing with the sacrifice of knowledge — as one, as distinct, in many ways — him who faces in all directions (9.15).
notes: Chapter 9 names the practice without further method; its other Gītā occurrences lie outside this chunk.

name: Repeated study of the science of the self
method_summary: Study and retention of the science of the self, practised constantly as study, listening and reflection.

name: The eighty-four postures of the Jogapradīpikā (group entry)
method_summary: The Brajbhāṣā Jogapradīpikā (18th c.) teaches eighty-four postures, alongside mudrās and other practices; the individual names are not recalled with enough confidence to be entered here.

name: The preliminaries of the Jonang vajra-yoga
method_summary: The common and uncommon preliminaries (refuge, bodhicitta, purification, maṇḍala offering, guru yoga) done in the Kālacakra form before the six-branch yoga is taught (details not recalled).
prerequisites: Kālacakra empowerment

name: Jukai (receiving the precepts)
method_summary: Ceremony of receiving the bodhisattva precepts (in Sōtō the sixteen: three refuges, three pure precepts, ten grave precepts) with a lineage chart (kechimyaku).

name: Jyotiṣṭoma (the model soma sacrifice)
method_summary: The archetypal soma rite ('one desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma'), whose basic form is the Agniṣṭoma; Śabara names it as the paradigm of what leads to the highest good.

name: Initiation into the Kabīr Panth
method_summary: Initiation by a mahant or ācārya with the giving of the Name and the kaṇṭhī necklace; in the Dharamdāsī line also the pān-parvānā; vows of vegetarianism and abstinence from intoxicants.

sources.ref: on the true Name and the pān-parvānā

name: Atiśa's daily conduct of a bodhisattva
method_summary: Rising in the last part of the night and recollecting the nature of phenomena; seeing appearances as illusion; seven-limb practice and aspiration; eating moderately with the body regarded as a boat and food divided in four offerings; circumambulation and recitation; the ten dharma practices with mindfulness; resting the mind free of elaboration in the first part of the night; sleeping in the lion posture with the notion of light.

name: Examining the mind day and night (Kadam self-watching)
method_summary: Checking one's mind-stream three times by day and three by night, proclaiming one's own faults, watching speech in company and mind when alone; the Kadam hermit Ben Gungyal counted his virtuous and non-virtuous thoughts with white and black pebbles.
notes: The pebble anecdote of Ben Gungyal is recalled from lojong and lamrim literature, not tied here to a verse.

name: The sixteen drops of the Kadam (bka' gdams thig le bcu drug)
method_summary: A guru-yoga visualisation of nested drops containing the lineage teachers, Kadam deities and the practitioner, taught in the Book of Kadam as the Kadam heart practice.
notes: Recalled only in outline; details not recorded.

name: Practice of the Eight Herukas (bka' brgyad)
method_summary: Sādhanas of the eight heruka classes, singly or gathered in one maṇḍala (as in Nyangral's Kagye Deshek Düpa).

name: Service (kainkarya) to the Lord
method_summary: Service of the Lord in temple and home — making garlands, cleaning, cooking offerings, singing — done for his pleasure alone, the natural expression of the soul's being his servant.

name: Kākī mudrā ('the crow')
method_summary: The mouth is shaped like a crow's beak and air is drunk in slowly (GS 3.86-87). The same 'crow's-beak' drinking of cool air is taught in the Śivasaṃhitā at the two twilights and day and night (ŚS 3.70, 3.74-75), and kākī is the means of filling the belly with air in vātasāra and bahiṣkṛta dhauti (GS 1.15, 1.22) and of drawing in prāṇa in yoni mudrā (GS 3.38).
signs_of_progress: destroys all diseases; one becomes free of disease like a crow (GS 3.86-87)
destroys consumption (ŚS 3.74)

warnings.text: Kākī is secret in all the tantras.

name: Kālajñāna (foreknowing the time of death)
method_summary: Reading signs in the breath, the body, shadows and dreams to foreknow the approach of death, so that one may prepare with equanimity and, if appropriate, undertake the final renunciation.
notes: Restricted/summary only: no omen-lists recorded.

name: Traditional study with the teacher (kālakṣepa)
method_summary: Study of the Śrībhāṣya, the Gītābhāṣya, the Tiruvāymoḻi commentaries and the rahasya works at the feet of a teacher of the lineage, orally, in the traditional order.

name: Skull-eating and corpse-ash practices (reported)
method_summary: Summary only: opponents report that the Kālāmukhas eat from a skull, bathe in the ash of corpses and eat it, and carry a club, as means to seen and unseen ends.

warnings.text: Yāmuna declares these acts forbidden by every scripture.

name: Comprehension by groups (kalāpa-sammasana)
method_summary: Applying the three characteristics to formations grouped by aggregate, period and so on — 'impermanent in the sense of destruction, painful in the sense of terror, not-self in the sense of coreless' — the beginning of full understanding as investigation.

name: Pot-consecration and bathing (kalaśābhiṣeka)
method_summary: Water is consecrated in arrays of pots in which deities are invoked and then poured over the image, to renew its power or to purify after pollution (e.g. sahasrakalaśa in Kerala).

name: Cheating death (kālavañcana)
method_summary: The texts' means of postponing or conquering death: breath held in the body (HYP 2.39–40), preserving bindu and nectar, the element-concentrations that remove fear of each element (DYŚ 100–110), and (HTK) knowledge of the signs of approaching death to anticipate it.

name: Kālī-pūjā
method_summary: The worship of Dakṣiṇakālī on the new-moon night of Kārttika (Dīpānvitā) in Bengal, in homes and public pandals and at temples such as Dakshineswar and Kalighat, with the Tantrasāra's meditation and mantras; also weekly and monthly worship.
notes: The spread of public Kālī-pūjā is traditionally credited to Rājā Kṛṣṇacandra of Nadia (18th c.) — tradition's account, not checked.

name: Public reading of the Kalpa Sūtra
method_summary: During Paryuṣaṇa a mendicant reads and explains the Kalpa Sūtra (with the Subodhikā or similar commentary) to the congregation over several days; the reading of Mahāvīra's birth, with the display of the fourteen dreams, is a festive high point; on Saṃvatsarī the Prakrit 'Bārasa Sūtra' is recited.

name: Good friendship (kalyāṇamittatā), the teacher who gives the subject
method_summary: Vism III: the meditation subject is taken from a good friend (kalyāṇamitta), described by a verse as dear, respected, esteemed (bhāvanīya), a speaker, patient with speech, able to speak on the profound and not urging to what is unfit; the Buddha is the best, then an arahant of the eighty great disciples, then a non-returner down to a one-Piṭaka holder who is conscientious (lajjī) and holds the teachers' tradition. Approach with the proper duties, ask at the proper time, state one's own temperament truthfully, and surrender oneself to the Buddha or the teacher; the teacher, knowing or asking the pupil's temperament, teaches the subject that suits it.

alt_method_summary: Associating with good friends and the wise, who are the whole of the holy life (SN 45.2; Ud 4.1; Snp 2.4).

name: Meditation on the kāmakalā
method_summary: Meditation on the Goddess's kāmakalā form — the point as face, the two points below and the triangle — taught in the Saundaryalaharī for the power to attract and in the Kāmakalāvilāsa as knowledge of the Śiva-Śakti union that liberates. Summary only.
prerequisites: initiation (dīkṣā) from a qualified guru into the relevant vidyā

warnings.text: The sixty-four tantras aimed at particular powers beguile the world; the Goddess's own tantra aims at all the ends of life.

name: Eating and drinking from the skull bowl
method_summary: The Aghora ascetic uses a skull (khappar) as his bowl, as a discipline of non-discrimination; the Kaulajñānanirṇaya calls the skull the best of vessels.

warnings.text: Aghora practice is given only by the guru and kept secret; the recent teacher Aghoreśvar Bhagavān Rām is reported to have taught that it is naturalness and service, not spectacle (the lineage's oral rule as reported; no text located — to be sourced).

name: Kapālabhāti / bhālabhāti (the skull-shining)
method_summary: In the Haṭhapradīpikā, rapid exhalation and inhalation like a blacksmith's bellows (HYP 2.35). In the Gheraṇḍa bhālabhāti is threefold: vāmakrama (breathing through alternate nostrils, not forcefully), vyutkrama (water drawn in through the nose and expelled through the mouth) and śītkrama (water sucked in through the mouth and expelled through the nose) (GS 1.55-60).
signs_of_progress: dries up the disorders of phlegm (HYP 2.35; GS 1.55)

warnings.text: One with excess fat or phlegm should first practise the six acts; others should not do them, their doṣas being in balance.
Some teachers hold that all impurities are dried up by breath-control alone and do not approve of the other acts.
The six acts, which purify the body, are to be kept secret.

name: Kapālarandhra-dhauti (rubbing the forehead hollow)
method_summary: The hollow at the forehead (bhālarandhra) is rubbed with the right thumb, on waking, after meals and at the end of the day (GS 1.34-35).
signs_of_progress: removes phlegm; the channels become clean and divine sight arises (GS 1.34-35)

name: Kapila's eight-limbed yoga with meditation on the Lord's form
method_summary: Duty, contentment, service of self-knowers, moderate pure food, solitude, the yamas and niyamas, posture, gradual mastery of breath, withdrawal, holding breath in one of its seats with the mind, meditation on the Lord's form limb by limb, and samādhi.

queries: local texts at the refs cited by prc:kapila-astanga-dhyana
checks.note: Rests on tea:kapila-gita:3.28.1-7, tea:kapila-gita:3.28.12-33; each was located in the local text and matches this entry's statement.

signs_of_progress: melting heart, hair standing on end, the mind attaining nirvāṇa like a flame (3.28.34-35)

name: Karaṇa: bodily seals in the āṇava means
method_summary: Āṇava immersion through karaṇa - bodily postures and seals (mudrā) - one of the five āṇava supports listed in MVT 2.21 and TĀ 1.170; treated in TĀ 5 and 32.
notes: Summary only; details of the karaṇas not recorded.

name: Karma-yoga: performing one's duty without attachment to the fruit
method_summary: Perform the prescribed action (one's own dharma) as duty, with evenness in success and failure, abandoning attachment and the desire for the fruit; action so done 'for the sake of sacrifice' does not bind and purifies the self.
stage: all; for the one wishing to ascend to yoga action is the means (6.3)
prerequisites: knowledge of one's own dharma (3.35)
signs_of_progress: evenness (samatva) in success and failure; freedom from the sense of doership (5.8–9)

warnings.text: Attachment to inaction is also forbidden.
One who restrains the organs of action but dwells on objects in mind is a hypocrite.
Action other than for the sake of sacrifice binds the world (3.9).
Do not let your attachment be to inaction.
Actionlessness is not attained by not undertaking actions, nor perfection by renunciation alone.
Restraining the organs of action while the mind dwells on sense-objects is hypocrisy (mithyācāra).
The wise should not unsettle the understanding of the ignorant who are attached to action.
The unyoked one, attached to the fruit through the drive of desire, is bound (5.12).

alt_method_summary: Undertake action with the organs of action, the senses controlled by the mind, without attachment (3.7); do the allotted action (niyataṃ karma), since action is better than inaction (3.8); act for the sake of sacrifice, free from attachment (3.9); keep one's entitlement to the action and not to its fruit, the fruit not being the motive (2.47); act established in yoga, the same in success and failure (2.48); act, as the knower does, for holding the world together (3.20, 3.25).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: do the action that is to be done without depending on its fruit (6.1), abandoning attachment and the fruit (4.20, 5.12), placing actions in Brahman (5.10), acting with body, mind, intellect and senses for purification of the self (5.11), for the sake of sacrifice (4.23), as the ancient seekers of liberation did (4.15). Declared superior to the renunciation of action (5.2).
Bhagavad Gītā 13.25: some see the self by karma-yoga, as others by meditation or sāṃkhya-yoga.

name: Karmamudrā (union with a consort)
method_summary: Summary only: sexual yoga with a qualified consort as a method of the higher consecrations and completion stage, to generate the gnosis of bliss and emptiness; the texts require consecration and pledges and warn against attachment. No procedure recorded.
prerequisites: the higher consecrations
pledges
for monastics: excluded (Atiśa)

warnings.text: The deluded who, attached to the bliss of union, call it the ultimate are like one who asks for news of Kāmarūpa at his own door.
The secret and wisdom consecrations are not to be taken by celibates; doing so destroys their vows and leads to bad destinies.
Tilopa: the gnosis arises only when there is no attachment (de la zhen med).
The heedless, those driven by craving, dependent on another and intoxicated fall from the meaning and again to the lower realms.
The method-path instruction is not given to all; it is sealed three times.
The secret and wisdom empowerments must not be taken by celibates; one who does breaks the vow of austerity, incurs defeat, falls to the lower realms and gains no accomplishment.

alt_method_summary: Kagyu contribution: in some lists one of Nāropa's dharmas, the 'method path'; sealed and restricted; summary only.

Summary only: completion-stage yoga with a consort, belonging to the higher empowerments. The Kadam and Gelug traditions restrict it: celibate monastics may not take the secret and wisdom empowerments literally, and Gelug monks practise with a visualised consort.
notes: U44 owns the Indian practice entry; this adds the Kagyu sources and warnings.

name: Invoking the Karmapa ('Karmapa khyenno')
method_summary: Repetition of the invocation 'Karmapa, think of me', a devotional mantra of the Karma Kagyu.

name: Relinquishing the fruit of all actions
method_summary: Giving up the fruit of all actions, self-controlled and taking refuge in the Lord's yoga — the step for one unable even to work for the Lord (12.11), praised above meditation because peace follows immediately (12.12), and what the wise call tyāga (18.2, 18.11).

alt_method_summary: Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: If unable to do even the Lord's work: resorting to his yoga, self-restrained, relinquish the fruit of all actions (12.11). It is then ranked above meditation (which is above knowledge, which is above practice), and peace follows relinquishment immediately (12.12).

Abandoning attachment to the fruit of action, ever content and depending on nothing, one does nothing though engaged in action (4.20); the yoked one who gives up the fruit attains lasting peace, while the unyoked, attached to fruit through desire, is bound (5.12); the renouncer and yogin acts without depending on the fruit (6.1).
signs_of_progress: Peace immediately (tyāgāc chāntir anantaram, 12.12).
notes: The commentators divide on how the ranking of 12.12 relates to 12.11's placing of relinquishment as the step for the least able.

name: Ear-splitting (kān-phaṛāī)
method_summary: At the second initiation the cartilage of both ears is split by a specialist guru and, after healing, the large earrings (darśan/mudrā) are inserted — the defining mark of the Kānphaṭa yogī. Summary only.

warnings.text: A bodily rite performed only by the guru within the order; not a practice to be undertaken by oneself (tradition's rule as reported).

prerequisites: first initiation and probation
notes: Body-cutting rite: summary only per project rules.

name: Karṇa-dhauti (cleansing the ears)
method_summary: The openings of the ears are cleaned with the tips of the index and ring fingers (GS 1.33).
signs_of_progress: by daily practice the inner sound becomes manifest (GS 1.33)

name: Karṇavedha (ear-piercing)
method_summary: Piercing the child's ears, a later addition to the lists.

name: Herbal kaṟpam (kaṟpa mūlikai)
method_summary: Summary only: the use of particular herbs regarded as rejuvenating (the tradition names, among others, kaṭukkāy (chebulic myrobalan), nellikkāy (emblic), karicālai (false daisy) and vallārai), taken as a long regimen under a physician's direction. No doses or preparations recorded.

warnings.text: Kaṟpam is taken only after purging and under the prescribed regimen; the physician decides.

notes: Herb names recalled at moderate confidence; the full list of kaṟpa herbs is not reconstructed.

name: Kartābhajā initiation
method_summary: Initiation by a Mahāśay with the sect's secret mantra, after which the disciple (barātī) worships the Kartā, pays dues and keeps the teaching hidden behind outward custom.
notes: The mantra is secret and not recorded.

name: Development of compassion (karuṇā)
method_summary: Pervading the directions with a mind of compassion; abandons cruelty (MN 62; DN 13).
alt_method_summary: Developed first towards one in misery, then the dear, neutral and hostile; its near enemy is home-based grief, its far enemy cruelty.

warnings.text: Guard against the near enemy, which resembles the virtue, and the far enemy, its opposite.

equivalents.note: YS 1.33's maitrī, karuṇā, muditā, upekṣā as attitudes for calming the mind; the Visuddhimagga develops them to absorption

name: The kasiṇas
method_summary: Perceiving a totality — earth, water, fire, air, blue, yellow, red, white, space or consciousness — above, below, across, non-dual and immeasurable (AN 10.25); the commentaries build forty meditation subjects on them (U37).

name: The air kasiṇa (vāyo-kasiṇa)
method_summary: Gazing at the wind moving leaves or touching the body, the meditator repeats its name and adverts to it with eyes open and closed until the learning sign arises, then develops it away from the device until the counterpart sign and access appear, extends the sign, and reaches the four (Abhidhamma: five) jhānas; used as a basis for supernormal power (travelling with the speed of wind).
prerequisites: purified virtue
impediments severed
subject received from a teacher
signs_of_progress: learning sign
counterpart sign
access
jhāna

warnings.text: Keep to a suitable dwelling, food, company and posture, or the sign is lost.

equivalents.note: concentration on the elements in the Yoga/haṭha catalogue; different theory and goal

notes: Device details from memory (Vism V not read locally).

name: The blue kasiṇa (nīla-kasiṇa)
method_summary: Gazing at blue flowers or cloth or a coloured disk, the meditator repeats its name and adverts to it with eyes open and closed until the learning sign arises, then develops it away from the device until the counterpart sign and access appear, extends the sign, and reaches the four (Abhidhamma: five) jhānas; used as a basis for supernormal power (creating blue forms, darkness).

name: The earth kasiṇa (pathavī-kasiṇa), taking the learning sign (Vism IV p. 125)
method_summary: Vism IV p. 125: the meditator looks at the prepared disk with the eyes opened evenly (as when looking at one's face in a mirror), not too wide and not too little; does not reflect on the colour or the mark but sets the mind on the concept 'earth' (pathavī), repeating it, opening and closing the eyes by turns until the learning sign arises (seen with the eyes shut as clearly as with them open). After that he develops it in his own dwelling; if the young concentration is lost he returns to the place, takes the sign again and continues. As he does so the hindrances are suppressed, the defilements subside, the mind is concentrated by access concentration and the counterpart sign arises.

alt_method_summary: Singing or reciting the names and deeds of the Lord, alone or together; declared the fearless way for all (BhP 2.1.11) and the means of the Kali age that gives what meditation, sacrifice and worship gave in earlier ages (BhP 12.3.51-52; VP 6.2.17).
Great souls ever sing the Lord's praise, strive, and bow to him with devotion (9.14); with minds on him they enlighten one another and always speak of him, content and rejoicing (10.9).

Lineage contribution (Āḻvārs; Bhakti Sūtras): singing the Lord's names with the mouth while thinking of him with the mind and offering pure flowers (TP 5); the devotees roam the earth singing and dancing (TVM 5.2.1); the name 'Nārāyaṇa' sung as refuge (PTM 1.1); every decad's last verse promises its fruit to those who recite it. The Nārada Sūtra: hearing and singing the Lord's qualities are means even in worldly life (NBS 37); being sung of, he quickly manifests (NBS 80).
Bhagavad Gītā 7–9: The great-souled always glorify the Lord (kīrtayantaḥ), striving, firm in vows, bowing with devotion, ever yoked (9.14).

Vārkarī: kīrtan and bhajan on abhaṅgas with the name; Ekaśaraṇa: kīrtana from the Kīrtana-ghoṣā, with hearing the foremost of devotions; Rāmānandī: singing Rāma's qualities, which in Kali carries one across.

Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: with their thought (citta) on the Lord and their life-breaths gone into him, the devotees awaken one another and are always speaking of him (bodhayantaḥ parasparaṃ kathayantaś ca mām), and are content and delight; to those who so worship with love he gives the yoga of understanding (10.9–10); the world rejoices and delights in his glorification (prakīrti) (11.36).

name: Meditation on the centres (Kaula)
method_summary: Fixing the mind on a centre — the root, the brahma-knot, the heart, the throat, the palate, the forehead, the brahmarandhra — or on a lamp-flame in the sixty-four-petalled lotus, each with its own signs and powers.

warnings.text: To be given only to a devoted disciple tested (even for a year); kept secret from the deceitful, cruel and undevoted.

signs_of_progress: trembling, shaking, speech in tongues, spontaneous seals, frog-hopping, levitation, knowledge of past and future (KJN 14.16–19)

name: Placing the syllables for liberation (Kaula nyāsa)
method_summary: Placing seed-syllables on the anus, genitals, navel, mouth, nostrils, ears, eyes and forehead; for one in whom it is established, liberation is certain and at death the skull splits.

name: Kōan introspection (sanzen, kōan practice)
method_summary: Working on an assigned kōan in zazen and daily activity, presenting one's understanding to the teacher in private interview; after the first barrier (e.g. 'wu', the sound of one hand), a graded series of cases, capping phrases and verses deepens and tests insight.

warnings.text: Do not seek the meaning in the phrase or understand it by reasoning (Yuanwu; Dahui).
Bankei held that manufacturing doubt trades the buddha-mind for a doubt.

name: Non-killing (kollāmai)
method_summary: Refraining from taking any life and protecting all creatures, even at the cost of one's own life.
alt_method_summary: Not killing, tormenting or eating living beings, regarding them as one's own life (Pattirakiriyār 14); do not throw stones at birds or kill a frightened life (Kaṭuveḷi 25, 29).

name: Step recitation (kramapāṭha)
method_summary: Reciting overlapping pairs of words (ab, bc, cd …) so that both the words and their junctions are fixed; taught in the Prātiśākhyas.

warnings.text: A mantra wrong in accent or letter does not convey its meaning; as a verbal thunderbolt it harms the sacrificer, as 'Indra-śatru' did through a fault of accent.

name: Krama contemplation of the twelve Kālīs
method_summary: Contemplating every act of cognition as the sequence of the twelve Kālīs - emission, persistence, withdrawal and the nameless across object, means of knowledge and subject - until the sequence dissolves into the sequenceless (TĀ 4.148-172; Abhinavagupta's Kramastotra).

name: Feigned sleep and snoring (krāthana)
method_summary: While awake he acts as if asleep, making a snoring sound in the throat with the out-breath, so that people despise him.

warnings.text: Undertaken only after knowledge has been gained, impurity reduced and the teacher's permission obtained; the feigned acts must not conflict with the restraints (non-harming, celibacy etc.).

name: Krauñca-niṣadana (sitting like a curlew)

name: Kṛcchra penances
method_summary: Summary only: graded expiatory penances regulating food and water over a set period (Prājāpatya, Sāṃtapana, Atikṛcchra, Taptakṛcchra, Parāka) (MDh 11.211–215).

warnings.text: Penances are to be undertaken according to one's capacity and under the direction of learned authorities; the digests allow substitutes for those unable to perform them.

name: Bathing in the Krīm Kuṇḍ
method_summary: Bathing in the tank at Kīnārām Sthal, Varanasi, held to cure illness and grant blessings, especially on set days.

method_summary: Austerity (tapas), self-study (svādhyāya) and devotion to Īśvara (YS 2.1): for the practitioner whose mind is not yet concentrated. Practised, it brings samādhi into being and thins the afflictions, making them like burnt seeds (YS 2.2, YBh 2.2).

signs_of_progress: afflictions thinned, like seeds burnt (YBh 2.2)

name: Kṣamāpanā (asking and granting forgiveness)
method_summary: Asking forgiveness of all beings and granting it, individually and collectively, especially on the last day of Paryuṣaṇa, with the words 'micchāmi dukkaḍaṃ'.

name: Kṣitigarbha recitation and offerings for the dead
method_summary: Reciting Kṣitigarbha's name and sūtra and making offerings during the forty-nine days after a death.

name: The 'razor' concentration (kṣurikā)
method_summary: A concentration that 'cuts' through the vital points and channels with mind and breath; summary only.

name: The dog-vow and the cow-vow
method_summary: Ascetics who live in the manner of a dog (eating food thrown on the ground, curling up like a dog) or of a cow, hoping for heavenly rebirth.

warnings.text: Perfected, the vow leads to rebirth among dogs or cattle; joined with the belief that it leads to godhood, it is wrong view leading to hell or the animal realm.

name: Kukkuṭāsana (the cockerel)
method_summary: From padmāsana the hands are inserted between the knees and thighs, planted on the ground, and the body raised into the air (HYP 1.23; GS 2.31).
prerequisites: padmāsana

name: Kula worship (the 'primal sacrifice') as interpreted by Abhinavagupta
method_summary: The secret Kaula ritual of Tantrāloka 29, in which worship with a consort and the Kaula substances is presented as the outward form of the union of Śiva and Śakti in consciousness. Summary only; no procedure is given here.

warnings.text: Presented as the secret rite (rahasya) for qualified initiates only.

notes: Restricted (sexual rite).

name: Worship of young girls as the Goddess (kumārī-pūjā)
method_summary: Young girls are honoured and fed as living forms of the Goddess, especially during Navarātri.
alt_method_summary: A young girl is worshipped as the living Goddess (in the eastern tantras, at Kāmākhyā and in the Bengal Durgā-pūjā).
notes: Detailed rules (age-names of the kumārī etc.) not recorded here; not checked.

name: The retentions of the Kumbhakapaddhati (group entry)
method_summary: RESTRICTED — existence and scope only: Raghuvīra's Kumbhakapaddhati is a manual devoted to breath-retention that describes many more kinds of kumbhaka than the Haṭhapradīpikā's eight. Their names and methods are not recorded here.

warnings.text: As a lion, an elephant or a tiger is tamed only slowly, so the breath must be brought under control gradually; otherwise it kills the practitioner.
Proper breath-control destroys all disease; improper practice produces all disease — hiccup, asthma, cough and pains in the head, ears and eyes arise from the disturbed breath.
Draw the breath in slowly and release it slowly; do not hold it excessively nor release it quickly.

notes: Group entry; the individual retentions are a Phase-D target (names only, methods restricted).

name: Matching horoscopes for marriage
method_summary: The asterisms and signs of bride and groom are compared under the eight heads (varṇa, vaśya, tārā, yoni, grahamaitra, gaṇa, bhakūṭa, nāḍī) worth 1 to 8 points, 36 in all, and faults such as nāḍī-doṣa and the fault of Mars are checked and their cancellations considered before the match and the wedding-moment are fixed.

name: Raising Kuṇḍalinī through the six centres (Śākta)
method_summary: The Goddess coiled at the root is awakened and led with the jīva up through the six centres to unite with Śiva in the thousand-petalled lotus, then led back (Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa 51-53). Summary only; taught as depending on the guru.

warnings.text: The practitioner is to be 'devoted to the guru's lotus feet' (the text's own qualification).

name: Kunye (bsku mnye) oil massage
method_summary: Massage with warmed oils, especially for rlung disorders, the elderly and in daily conduct (method details not recorded).

equivalents.note: oil massage

name: Kūrmāsana (the tortoise seat)
method_summary: The anus closed firmly with the ankles placed in reverse order (HYP 1.22); in the Gheraṇḍa the ankles crossed under the scrotum with body, head and neck straight (GS 2.32).

name: The kusāli's accumulation (offering the body)
method_summary: The renunciant's offering: visualizing one's consciousness as a wrathful ḍākinī who cuts off the body's skull as a cauldron, transforms the body into nectar and offers it to the buddhas and to all guests, cutting attachment to the body. A visualization only; related to Chöd (owned by U48).

name: Hut-entering rejuvenation (kuṭīprāveśika)
method_summary: The principal mode of rasāyana: after preliminary rites, with shaved head, steadied resolve and a mind freed of its doṣas and turned to friendliness toward beings, the person enters a specially built secluded hut, is purified by cleansing therapies and then takes the rejuvenative under a physician's care. Summary only: construction, diet, preparations and durations are not recorded.

warnings.text: The better mode but very hard to carry out; only for the capable and self-controlled.
Diseases arising from lapses in the regimen are to be treated apart from the rasāyana.

prerequisites: capacity, health, wisdom, self-control, leisure and means (Ci 1.4.27)
notes: Marked restricted because the full regimen involves prolonged seclusion, purgation and special diet, and some formulations include metals and gems (e.g. Ci 1.4.22).

name: Contemplation of the three targets (lakṣya-traya)
method_summary: Attending to the inner target (kuṇḍalinī, inner sound, blue light), the outer target (colours and lights in space) and the intermediate target (voids).
signs_of_progress: lights, stars, a diamond mirror, the full moon, the midday sun, a flame (Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa 2.1)

queries: e-text refs of prc:laksya-traya
checks.note: The inline refs and paraphrased content were checked against the e-text passages read for the teachings. All 2 teachings it rests on exist and were located in the e-text.

alt_method_summary: The Vivekamārtaṇḍa asks how yogins can succeed who do not know in their own body the six centres, the sixteen supports, the three targets (lakṣya) and the five voids; the Haṭhapradīpikā's śāmbhavī is defined by the 'inner target' held while the gaze is outward (HYP 4.36-37). The fuller teaching of the inner, outer and intermediate targets is in the Advayatāraka and Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa Upaniṣads and the Siddhasiddhāntapaddhati.
notes: Contributes haṭha/Nāth sources to U04's entry; see U28's cpt:three-laksyas.

name: Contemplation of the Goddess as kuṇḍalinī
method_summary: Contemplation of the Goddess rising from the base through the cakras, piercing the three knots, uniting with her consort in the crown, showering nectar over the body and returning to sleep coiled at the base, as described in the Sahasranāma and the Saundaryalaharī; in the Kalpasūtra's morning routine the nectar flows from the guru's feet in the crown. Summary only.
prerequisites: initiation (dīkṣā) from a qualified guru into the relevant vidyā

warnings.text: Those without the succession of teachers, proud of mere knowledge, are harmed by the mantra's rays through their breach of the samaya.
The mind's steady flow toward the meaning comes only by the guru's grace, not by scripture alone.

signs_of_progress: nectar felt flowing from the crown (SL 10; LSN 39)
the Goddess seen as a streak of lightning above the six lotuses by the pure-minded (SL 21)

name: Recitation of the Lalitā Sahasranāma
method_summary: Daily recitation of the thousand names, often with the introductory and concluding parts; Bhāskararāya treats it as a daily duty that can also serve desired ends; the Rudrayāmala (as he quotes it) places name-recitation at the summit of a ladder of births leading to liberation while living.

warnings.text: The concluding section restricts the hymn to devotees of Lalitā (as summarized; low confidence).

name: Lamdre contemplation of the three visions
method_summary: Contemplating in order the impure vision (sufferings of saṃsāra, the difficulty of leisure and endowment, death, karma), the experiential vision (love, compassion, relative and ultimate bodhicitta, and the experiences of meditation) and the pure vision (the qualities of buddhahood) as the preliminary of the Lamdre.

name: Meditation on the stages of the path
method_summary: Daily sessions in which, after the six preparatory practices, one takes one lamrim topic (the teacher, leisure and endowment, death, the lower realms, refuge, karma, saṃsāra's faults, the twelve links, bodhicitta, the perfections, calm, insight) as the subject of analytical meditation until a felt conviction arises, then holds it with placement meditation; ends with dedication; the whole cycle is repeated.

name: Practice with a consort (latā-sādhana)
method_summary: The Kaula rite with a female partner (latā). Restricted: named only; the Mahānirvāṇa limits it to one's own wife in the Kali age.

warnings.text: In the Kali age only one's own wife.
Taking a woman by force leads to the Raurava hell.
Women are goddesses; never to be struck, reviled or deceived.

name: The four dissolutions (Aṣṭāvakra Gītā)
method_summary: Recognizing 'I am like space, the world a pot', 'I am the ocean, the world its waves', 'I am the shell, the world the imagined silver', 'I am in all beings and they in me' — after which nothing is to be renounced, accepted or dissolved.

name: The 'signals' of laya-yoga (saṅketa)
method_summary: Laya-yoga is the dissolution of the mind brought about by any of the 'signals' Ādinātha taught — eight crore of them: meditating on the void while walking, standing, sleeping and eating; gazing at the nose-tip; meditating on the back of the head (said to conquer death); gazing between the brows; attending to the forehead; to the big toes; lying like a corpse, relaxed, in a solitary place (DYŚ 14-24). The Haṭhapradīpikā similarly speaks of a crore and a quarter ways of laya, nāda being chief (HYP 4.66).
signs_of_progress: dissolution of the mind (cittalaya) (DYŚ 14, 24)
alt_method_summary: Dissolving the mind by fixing attention on an 'indication': meditating on the void at all times, gazing at the nose-tip or between the brows, meditating on the back of the head or on the big toes, lying relaxed like a corpse in solitude — Ādinātha taught eight crore such (DYŚ 14–24).

name: Learning from all beings (the avadhūta's method)
method_summary: Observing the ways of the elements, animals and people and drawing from each a lesson for detachment and knowledge, as the avadhūta took twenty-four teachers and his own body as a twenty-fifth.

name: Ledi Sayadaw's lay insight method
method_summary: Establishing mindfulness of breathing (or of the body), then contemplating the four elements, feelings and the aggregates as impermanent, suffering and not-self, supported by study of the Abhidhamma manuals; offered to laypeople.

name: The 'liberation' rite (sgrol ba)
method_summary: A wrathful tantric rite in which the consciousness of a being causing great harm is, by tradition, liberated into a pure realm, performed on an effigy (liṅga). Recorded as a summary only.

warnings.text: Tradition allows it only to one who can actually transfer the consciousness to a pure realm and acts out of compassion; performed otherwise it is a grave downfall that harms the performer.

notes: RESTRICTED: no procedure recorded.

name: Liberation through hearing (thos grol)
method_summary: Reading the Bardo Thödol aloud to the dying and dead, from the moment of death through the forty-nine days, introducing the clear light and the deities and guiding the consciousness.

name: Remembering the incarnations' deeds
method_summary: Reading, reciting and meditating on the episodes of the Līḷācaritra and the lives of the five Kṛṣṇas as the devotee's constant remembrance.

name: Offering all enjoyment to the liṅga (arpaṇa)
method_summary: Whatever is set aside for one's own enjoyment — food, sights, sounds — is first offered to the liṅga and then received as its grace.

name: Wearing the liṅga (liṅgadhāraṇa)
method_summary: The iṣṭaliṅga, kept in a small casket (karaḍige) on a cord, is worn on the body at all times — at the head, throat, chest, armpit, belly or in the hand, never below the navel; inwardly the liṅga of light is held in the mind at the base, heart or brows.

warnings.text: Never separate the liṅga from the body at any time or place.
Wearing it below the navel is a cause of sin; not on the tip of matted hair, lower back or an unclean place.
The text treats the liṅga's accidental fall with the utmost gravity (recorded as restricted).

name: Liṅga-initiation (liṅgadīkṣā)
method_summary: The guru, with assistants, bathes the disciple with water from pots consecrated by the five brahma-mantras, whispers the five-syllable mantra secretly into the right ear, installs a purified liṅga in the disciple's life-breath and places it in his hand to be worn for life. In Liṅgāyata practice it is given to all, women and children included.
prerequisites: a qualified guru (SSM 6.1–6); the disciple's discernment and dispassion

warnings.text: The mantra is given secretly (nigūḍham).

name: Worship of the liṅga
method_summary: Worship of Śiva in the formless liṅga (including liṅgas made of earth for the occasion), with bathing, bilva leaves, lamps and offerings; the Śiva Purāṇa teaches that Śiva alone may be worshipped in the liṅga because he alone is niṣkala.

name: Burial of the dead as liṅgaikya
method_summary: The dead devotee, having become one with the liṅga, is buried seated with the liṅga in hand rather than cremated; no death-pollution or ancestral rites are observed.
notes: Community practice from general knowledge; verify the details (posture, rites) in Phase C.

name: Sleeping in the lion posture
method_summary: Lying on the right side like a lion (as the Buddha at his passing), with the notion of rising and of light, falling asleep in virtue.

name: Metal transmutation (lohavedha / dhātuvāda)
method_summary: The transformation of base metals by processed mercury, treated in the 'vāda' sections of the rasa texts and regarded as a test to be passed before mercury is applied to the body. RESTRICTED: summary only.

warnings.text: Rasa-śāstra is not to be taken as merely for metallurgy; its purpose is liberation through the body.
Mercury with its impurities, though nectar itself, is poison; a physician skilled in practice but ignorant of the science is death in human form.

name: Mind training (blo sbyong)
method_summary: Training the mind in relative and ultimate bodhicitta by means of short slogans applied throughout the day: after the preliminaries, meditating on phenomena as dream-like and resting in the mind's nature (ultimate), practising sending and taking on the breath (relative), turning every adversity into the path, applying the five powers in life and at death, checking one's progress, and keeping the commitments and precepts.
prerequisites: refuge
the four thoughts that turn the mind
some understanding of bodhicitta
signs_of_progress: one can practise even when distracted (Seven Points 5.4)
a constantly joyful mind (5.3)
one's own mind as the principal witness (5.2)
self-cherishing lessens (5.1)

warnings.text: Do not let the gods descend into demons — mind training that increases pride is inverted.
Abandon poisoned food — virtue mixed with self-grasping.
Do not act with a twist — practising mind training for selfish ends.

equivalents.note: lojong includes and systematises Śāntideva's exchange

name: Mind-training transference at death (the five powers)
method_summary: At death one gives away one's possessions (white seed), confesses and purifies, and applies the five powers — resolve, familiarity, white seed, repudiation, aspiration — lying in the lion posture and practising sending and taking, then resting in the nature of mind.
notes: Details follow the commentaries, recalled.

name: Long-life practice (tshe sgrub)
method_summary: Sādhana of long-life deities (Amitāyus, Padmasambhava as Tsepakme with Mandāravā) to extend life and restore vitality.

name: Looking at the mind (Mahāmudrā vipaśyanā)

names.name: sems la lta ba; gnas 'gyu rig gsum

method_summary: In stillness and in movement the meditator looks for the mind: its colour, shape, location, where it arises, abides and goes, whether the still and moving mind are one or different; not finding anything, recognizes the unfindable, luminous nature.

equivalents.note: both are direct inquiries into the knower; the Advaita inquiry seeks the Self, the Kagyu looking finds no self and recognizes emptiness-clarity — the traditions insist on this difference

name: Lotus repentance and Samantabhadra visualization
method_summary: Repentance of the six senses before Samantabhadra, reciting the Lotus, contemplating the true mark; Samantabhadra appears on his white elephant to the reciter.
notes: Tiantai's 'Lotus samādhi' ritual (Zhiyi) belongs to U54.

name: The honey-doctrine (madhu-vidyā)
method_summary: ChU 3.1-11: meditate on the sun as the honey of the gods, the Vedas as flowers and the rays as honeycomb cells; for one who knows it the sun neither rises nor sets. BAU 2.5 (also called the madhu-brāhmaṇa): meditate on earth, waters, fire and all things as 'honey' for all beings and all beings as honey for them, culminating in 'this self is brahman'.

warnings.text: To be taught only to one's eldest son or a worthy pupil (ChU 3.11.5-6).

notes: Upaniṣadic 'vidyā' (meditation-knowledge); the Brahma Sūtra (3.3) discusses which vidyās are to be combined.

name: Bee-like alms (mādhukarī)
method_summary: The renunciant takes a little food from many houses without burdening any and stores nothing for later.

alt_method_summary: Taking a little food from several houses after the household cooking fires are out, never from a single house; eating moderately (half food, a quarter water, a quarter air).

name: Unfolding of the centre (madhyavikāsa)
method_summary: The bliss of consciousness is gained by the unfolding of the centre - the central consciousness, the suṣumnā of the breath, the gap between states - through the means listed in PH 18.

name: Mahābandha (the great lock)
method_summary: With the left heel at the perineum and the right foot on the left thigh, the breath is filled, the chin set firmly on the chest, the perineum contracted and the mind fixed in the middle; the breath is held as far as able and released slowly, on both sides (HYP 3.19-21; ŚS 4.21-22; DYŚ 123). In the Gheraṇḍa the left ankle blocks the anus and the right foot presses that ankle, with jālandhara (GS 3.18-20). Some teachers replace the throat lock here with the tongue pressed at the root of the front teeth (HYP 3.22).
signs_of_progress: stops the upward movement in all channels; releases death's noose; brings about the confluence of the three rivers and leads the mind to Kedāra (HYP 3.23-24)
the breath enters the middle of the suṣumnā; the body is nourished (ŚS 4.22)

warnings.text: Mahāmudrā and mahābandha are fruitless without mahāvedha.

name: Mahābandha and mahāvedha
method_summary: Combined locks and the 'great piercing' named in the Yogatattva; summary only.

name: Mahākāla protector practice (Kagyu)
method_summary: Daily and annual rituals to the protector — Bernagchen for the Karma Kagyu, six-armed Mahākāla for the Shangpa — to remove obstacles to practice.

name: The great head-anointing of Bāhubali
method_summary: About every twelve years the 58-foot image of Bāhubali at Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa is anointed from a scaffold with water, milk, sugarcane juice, sandal, saffron and other substances, in memory of his renunciation and standing meditation.

name: Repetition of the Mahāmṛtyuñjaya (Tryambaka) verse
method_summary: In jyotiṣa, the recitation prescribed again and again as the remedy for periods and sub-periods threatening untimely death (a planet ruling the 2nd or 7th), together with a pacification pleasing to the planet and gifts (BPHS 52–60).
alt_method_summary: Repeating and offering with the verse 'we worship Tryambaka … may I be freed from death, not from immortality' for release from death and for health; in the Yajurveda it accompanies the Tryambaka offerings to Rudra.

Repeating, and offering into fire with, the verse to Tryambaka — 'we worship the three-eyed one, fragrant, increaser of prosperity; like a cucumber from its stalk may I be freed from death, not from immortality' (RV 7.59.12) — for release from untimely death and disease and for liberation; in the mantra manuals it is enlarged with Oṃ and seed-syllables and given with its seer, metre, deity and meditation on the three-eyed Śiva holding the jar of nectar, and is used in rites of pacification for the sick and dying.
notes: The seed-syllable forms of the manuals (e.g. with hauṃ juṃ saḥ) are recalled with low confidence and not given here.

name: Mahāmudrā (the great seal)
method_summary: Pressing the perineum with the left heel, the right leg stretched out and its foot held with the hands, the chin on the chest (throat lock), the breath filled and held upward, then released slowly; practised on the left side and then equally on the right (HYP 3.10-15; GS 3.6-8; ŚS 4.16-20; DYŚ 121-122; GŚ 33). The texts say kuṇḍalinī then straightens like a snake struck with a stick and a death-like state arises as the breath leaves the two channels (HYP 3.11-12). It is the first of the trio (with mahābandha and mahāvedha) taught already in the Amṛtasiddhi.

equivalents.note: same name, different practice: a bodily seal in haṭha, the resting of mind in its nature in the Buddhist siddhas

notes: U49 contribution: cross-family equivalents only (other fields copied unchanged).

signs_of_progress: destroys the great afflictions and death; all tastes become tasteless and even poison is digested like nectar; consumption, skin disease, constipation, gulma and indigestion vanish (HYP 3.14-17)
removes wrinkles, grey hair, old age and death, consumption, cough, fever (GS 3.8)

warnings.text: It is to be guarded with effort and not given to just anyone.
It is secret in all the tantras; to be practised as the guru teaches.
The ten mudrās are to be guarded like a jewel-box and told to no one.

alt_notes: Homonym only of the Buddhist mahāmudrā (Kagyu); no equivalence is asserted. U04's combined entry prc:mahabandha-mahavedha overlaps the next two entries.
alt_method_summary: The 'great seal' named among the haṭha practices of the Yogatattva and Dhyānabindu; recorded by name and purpose only.

name: Mahāmudrā as a hand-gesture (paramīkaraṇa)
method_summary: The thumbs interlocked and the fingers extended, shown to 'make supreme' (paramīkaraṇa) in the worship of the deity (ŚT 23.113-114); distinct from the haṭha mahāmudrā.

name: Mahāmudrā meditation (Kagyu)
method_summary: After the preliminaries and the guru's pointing-out, the meditator settles the mind (śamatha), looks directly at it (vipaśyanā), recognizes its empty and luminous nature, and sustains that recognition without contrivance or distraction in and between sessions, progressing through the four yogas.
prerequisites: the preliminaries (ngöndro)
the guru's pointing-out and blessing
signs_of_progress: experiences of bliss, clarity and non-thought (not to be clung to)
recognition of thoughts as mind's own display
the four yogas: one-pointedness, simplicity, one taste, non-meditation

warnings.text: The four deviations from emptiness and the three strayings into bliss, clarity and non-thought.
Without hope and fear the fruit is manifest; hope and fear themselves obstruct it.

notes: Not the haṭha 'mahāmudrā' seal (prc:mahamudra), which is a different practice with the same name.

name: Resting in mahāmudrā (the Indian siddha instruction)
method_summary: Cutting the root of one's own mind and leaving awareness naked; letting the muddy water of concepts clear; neither blocking nor affirming appearances; relaxing body, speech and mind; mind without aim; looking at the sky-like nature until 'seeing' ceases; amanasikāra — not engaging concepts.
prerequisites: the true guru's instruction
renunciation (Gaṅgāmā v2–3)

names.name: phyag rgya chen po / yid la mi byed pa

signs_of_progress: torrent, gentle river, ocean (Gaṅgāmā v21)
thoughts dissolve like clouds in space (v10)

warnings.text: For those of lesser intellect who cannot remain in the meaning, Tilopa prescribes working with the winds and gazes instead.
Arising intent obscures clear light; guarding vows conceptually degenerates the pledge.

name: Mahāmudrā śamatha with support
method_summary: The mind is rested on an object — a small pebble or stick, an image, the breath (counting or following), or a deity's form — without tightness or looseness, until it settles.

warnings.text: Too tight brings agitation, too loose dullness: balance them.

name: Mahāmudrā śamatha without support
method_summary: The mind rests without any object, letting thoughts subside in their own place, 'like waves returning to the ocean'.

name: The eightfold prognostication (mahānimitta)
method_summary: Divination from the year, dreams, bodily marks, portents, signs of the body and omens, to foretell gain and loss, pleasure and pain, life and death; Gosāla learned it from the six disācaras.

warnings.text: Some omens come true, for others the knowledge fails; it is not the way of release.

notes: Category 'ritual' is the nearest fit for a divinatory lore.

name: The Mahānubhāva renunciant discipline
method_summary: Monks and nuns keep moving (aṭana), live by begging, keep no possessions, harm no creature, avoid worldly company and remain in remembrance of Parameśvara and his incarnations.

name: The great departure (mahāprasthāna)
method_summary: Summary only: at the end of life the Pāṇḍavas renounce the kingdom and walk toward the north until the body falls (MBh 17.1–2). No instructions are given here.

warnings.text: The epic presents the departure as the close of a completed life after renunciation of kingship; each of the fallen is said to fall by his own fault, and only Yudhiṣṭhira reaches heaven in the body.
Later Dharmaśāstra authorities list the great departure among practices forbidden in the Kali age (kalivarjya).

name: Maharshi Mehi's graded practice
method_summary: Mental repetition (mānas jap), mental contemplation of form (mānas dhyān), fixing the gaze at a point (dṛṣṭi yoga) to open the inner light, and meditation on sound (nādānusandhān).

name: Noting (the Mahāsi method)
method_summary: Making a light mental note of every object as it arises — 'rising', 'falling', 'thinking', 'hearing', 'pain', 'intending' — in sitting, walking and all daily activities, to build continuous mindfulness and momentary concentration and see arising and passing.
signs_of_progress: the insight knowledges in sequence (Progress of Insight)

warnings.text: Lights, rapture and other experiences at the stage of arising and passing are to be noted, not taken for attainment.

name: Understanding the great saying
method_summary: Understanding 'that thou art' by first grasping the words' meanings and then, by partial implication, the consciousness common to 'that' and 'thou', with faith and the teacher's grace.

name: Mahāvedha (the great piercing)
method_summary: Seated in mahābandha with the breath filled and held by the throat seal, the hands placed evenly on the ground, the buttocks are gently struck on the ground so that the breath leaves the two side channels and throbs in the middle (HYP 3.26-28; ŚS 4.23; DYŚ 124, where the vulgate calls it mahābandha); in the Gheraṇḍa, a retention with uḍḍīyāna made in mahābandha (GS 3.22). Without it mahāmudrā and mahābandha are fruitless (HYP 3.25; GS 3.21; ŚS 4.27).
signs_of_progress: a death-like state; the union of moon, sun and fire (HYP 3.28)
removes wrinkles, grey hair and trembling; gives powers such as aṇimā (HYP 3.29-30)
the brahma-knot is pierced; the gods in the centres tremble; kuṇḍalinī dissolves in Kailāsa (ŚS 4.24-26)

warnings.text: These three (mahāmudrā, mahābandha, mahāvedha) are a great secret.
The best yogins keep this vedha secret.

name: Worship of a Mahāvidyā
method_summary: Worship of one of the ten Mahāvidyās by her mantra (received in initiation), yantra, meditation verse, placing of the mantra on the body and preparatory repetition (puraścaraṇa), with her Bhairava at her right (Toḍala 1.3-19; Tantrasāra).

warnings.text: The claim that Mahāvidyā mantras need no preliminary checks is praise; the checks are still to be made (a hostile mantra's fault has been seen).

name: Mahāvīra Jayantī
method_summary: The celebration of Mahāvīra's birth on the thirteenth of bright Caitra, with processions, worship and readings.

name: The great vow of the skull (mahāvrata, kapālavrata)
method_summary: Summary only: the ascetic lives as a skull-bearer - skull as begging-bowl, skull-topped staff, ash - in imitation of the Lord's penance; named 'beyond the world' for the Lākulas and the Kāpāla vow by opponents.

name: The great vows of the ascetic
method_summary: Lifelong, total abstention from violence, falsehood, stealing, sexual activity and possession, in thought, word and deed, by doing, causing and approving, supported by the twenty-five contemplations; Śvetāmbaras add not eating at night.
prerequisites: right view
initiation (dīkṣā)

name: Worship and service of devotees (Māhēśvara-pūjā)
method_summary: Feeding, serving and honouring Śiva's devotees as Śiva himself; the freed soul's conduct (Civañāṉa Pōtam 12) and the practice of many Nāyaṉmārs.
alt_method_summary: Tāyumāṉavar asks to be made a servant for the service of devotees, from which the state of bliss comes of itself.

name: Temple festival (mahotsava)
method_summary: The annual festival begun by hoisting the flag, with daily processions of the festival image, offerings to the attendant beings and a concluding bath (avabhṛtha/ārāṭṭu), conducted by the priest or tantri.
alt_method_summary: The annual festival: flag-hoisting, processions of the deity, and the concluding bath.

name: The four attitudes (maitrī, pramoda, kāruṇya, mādhyasthya)
method_summary: Cultivating friendliness to all beings ('may no one do evil, may no one suffer, may the world be freed'), joy at the virtues of others, compassion for the afflicted, and impartiality toward the incorrigible; recited in the Sāmāyikapāṭha and used to support meditation.

equivalents.note: Same four attitudes as Yoga Sūtra 1.33 with different objects.
same four attitudes; the Jain form assigns each to a class of beings, the Buddhist pervades all directions
as above

name: Makarāsana (the crocodile)
method_summary: Lying face down with the chest on the ground and the legs stretched out, the head held with the arms (GS 2.40).
signs_of_progress: increases the bodily fire (GS 2.40)

name: Reflection (manana)
method_summary: Reasoned reflection on what has been heard, removing doubts and contrary views — in Dvaita often in the company of fellow students and through the tradition's disputations.

name: Reflection (manana) by reasoning
method_summary: Examining by reasoning, after hearing scripture, what has been heard — above all about the Lord and the self; Udayana calls such reasoning itself a form of worship.

name: Mental repetition — mānasa japa
method_summary: Reciting inwardly, with the intellect, the series of the mantra's letters, notes and words while remembering its meaning, without moving head, tongue or lips; a thousand times better than ritual sacrifice.

name: Seeing the mind with the mind

name: Mental temple-building and worship

equivalents.note: inner worship as a sustained practice rather than a ritual segment

The mental offering of the upacāras to Kālī, as in the Mahānirvāṇa's inner worship.

name: Inner worship mapped onto the state beyond mind
method_summary: Each service of worship understood as a moment of the mind-less state — invocation as abandoning action, the lamp as the sun of consciousness, salutation as 'so'ham', praise as silence (Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa 2.2).

method_summary: Recitation of the deity's mantra — spoken, whispered or mental, counted in the 'service' (sevā) phase — joined with the visualization of the deity.

name: The ten purifications of a mantra (mantra-saṃskāra)
method_summary: Summary only: a defective or newly received mantra is made effective by ten rites — generation, enlivening, striking, awakening, consecration, cleansing, strengthening, satiation, kindling and guarding (secrecy) — performed according to the teacher's tradition (ŚT 2.112–123).

method_summary: Serving and worshipping the divine in human beings, above all in the living guru, instead of images; in Kartābhajā the guru (Mahāśay) as the Kartā's presence.

name: Mindfulness of death (maraṇassati)

sense of urgency
disenchantment
access

name: Loving-kindness (mettā-bhāvanā)
method_summary: Vism IX, from the opening to the breaking down of the barriers: the beginner, having cut impediments and taken the subject, sits at ease after the meal in a secluded place and first reflects on the danger in hate and the benefit of patience. Loving-kindness is developed first toward oneself ('may I be happy and free from suffering'), as one's own witness; then toward a dear and respected person; then, to break down the barriers, toward a very dear friend, a neutral person and an enemy, making the mind soft and workable at each step. It is not developed first toward a disliked person, a very dear friend, a neutral person or an enemy, not specifically toward one of the opposite sex, and not at all toward the dead. If resentment arises, the text gives an ordered set of remedies (prc:patigha-vinodana-vism). The barrier is broken when the mind is even toward oneself and the three others (the bandits test); then the sign and access arise, and absorption follows (the first jhāna accompanied by loving-kindness, and the higher ones), after which the directions are pervaded (Vism IX p. 307-308).

Cultivating a boundless heart towards all beings as a mother protects her only child, wishing 'may all beings be happy', standing, walking, sitting or lying down (Snp 1.8); keeping the mind of love even under the saw (MN 21).

equivalents.note: YS 1.33's maitrī, karuṇā, muditā, upekṣā as attitudes for calming the mind; the Visuddhimagga develops them to absorption

name: Recitation of the Migtsema
method_summary: Repeating the Migtsema praise of Tsongkhapa as a mantra, often within the Hundred Deities of Tuṣita guru yoga, with visualisations of nectar and light for purification and for gaining wisdom.

name: Searching for the mind (sems 'tshol)
method_summary: Examining where mind comes from, where it stays and where it goes, and what its colour and shape are, until its unfindability is seen; part of the secret rushen and of Bön Dzogchen preliminaries.

name: Moderate diet (mitāhāra) in the haṭha texts
method_summary: Agreeable, sweet, unctuous food leaving a quarter of the stomach empty, offered to Śiva (HYP 1.58); half the stomach filled with food, a quarter with water and a quarter left for the air (GS 5.21-22); avoiding the bitter, sour, pungent, salty and hot, reheated or dry food, liquor, fish and meat, garlic and asafoetida (HYP 1.59-61; GS 5.23-25; ŚS 3.33; DYŚ 64-65); favouring wheat, rice, barley, milk, ghee, honey, mung and pure water (HYP 1.62-63; GS 5.17-20, 5.27-29). At the start of practice milk and ghee are recommended (HYP 2.14; ŚS 3.37; GŚ 50). It is called the chief of the restraints (HYP 1.38).

Early bathing, fasting and other mortifications of the body are to be avoided.
Do not practise immediately after eating nor when very hungry.

Overeating is the first of the six things that destroy yoga.

alt_method_summary: Eating smooth, sweet, wholesome food, offered to Śiva, leaving a quarter (GS: half food, a quarter water, a quarter air) of the stomach empty; avoiding pungent, sour, salty, heating and stale foods, alcohol, meat and fish; milk and ghee at the start of practice (HYP 1.58–63, 2.14; GS 5.16–25; DYŚ 64–66).

Sweet, unctuous food eaten leaving a quarter of the stomach empty; avoiding the hot, sour, salty, pungent; wholesome milk, ghee, wheat, mung, rice; called the chief of the yamas (Yogatattva 28–29, 46–49; Yogacūḍāmaṇi 43).

name: Moderation in food, sleep, recreation and effort
method_summary: For one measured in food and recreation, measured in effort in actions, measured in sleep and waking, yoga becomes the destroyer of sorrow (6.17); yoga is not for one who eats too much, nor for one who does not eat at all, nor for one given to too much sleep, nor for one who keeps awake (6.16).
